title: Nvidia's most advanced AI chips reportedly reached US firms controlled by Chinese parents
subtitle: A November 27 report names RiCloud and Yuxing as US-registered companies whose parent entities sit in China, raising a loophole that the current export-control regime was meant to close and sharpening the questions Jensen Huang faces in Congress.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Yahoo Finance's technology desk reported on November 27 that Nvidia sold its most advanced AI chips to two US-registered companies, RiCloud and Yuxing, whose ultimate parent entities are headquartered in China. The story cites the companies' corporate structure rather than any accusation of wrongdoing: the US government has not charged either firm. It lands days before Jensen Huang's scheduled closed-door testimony before Congress, now expected in early December after an original Thanksgiving target passed.

The sales matter because the rule the Commerce Department issued earlier this year treats a subsidiary as part of its Chinese parent, whatever city it operates from. That rule was introduced after reporting on offshore rental loopholes and the Megaspeed entity-listing case, and it is the mechanism the Bureau of Industry and Security relies on to extend licensing requirements past the border. If chips cleared for sale to US companies ended up at entities whose parents are inside the controlled perimeter, the design assumption of the rule did not hold on first contact.

This is the third surface of the same diversion story in two weeks. Megaspeed's inclusion on the entity list named seven firms across Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. A separate BIS proposal would require export licenses for shipments to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil on diversion risk grounds. The RiCloud and Yuxing reports move the same conversation onto US soil — an accountability path for Washington that does not need a cooperating Southeast Asian regulator to work. It also hands the congressional committees preparing to question Huang a concrete compliance-process question that does not require arguing over foreign jurisdiction.

A note for learners: when a technology is subject to export control, where the chips physically sit matters less than whose instructions the chips obey. A compliance regime built on physical geography can be arbitraged by legal geography — standing up a US entity whose parent sits abroad — and arbitraged again by remote access, where the chips never move at all. Watching how BIS, Congress and Nvidia rewrite their control surface over the next twelve months is a live lesson in how technology policy adapts to the shape of the underlying system, or fails to.
